items.context: Booking a birthday dinner for six. One guest, Mia, is vegan.
items.question: Two places have a table Saturday at 7: Brasa, the steakhouse you loved, or Verde, which is fully vegan. Brasa has the better room; at Verde, Mia can order anything. So: 1) Verde, 2) Brasa?
options: Book Brasa, the steakhouse
Book Verde, the vegan place
Hold both tables and decide on Friday
Dinner at Brasa, then dessert at Verde
items.cue: "2nd one" follows the numbered recap, the latest and most explicit list, where 2 = Brasa.
items.explanation: The prose mentions Brasa first and Verde second, but the agent then restated the options with numbers. Ordinals bind to the most recent explicit enumeration, and "2nd one" echoes its numbering.
items.grounding: CLAMBER: weak use of contextual cues for references.

items.context: Renting a car for a weekend away.
items.question: For the car: the SUV, or the compact? I'd go with the compact, since it's just the two of you and parking in the old town is a nightmare.
options: The SUV, the first option
Reserve both and cancel one later
The compact, as recommended
Ask again, since "yep" doesn't pick one
items.cue: The agent's turn ended with a proposal ("I'd go with the compact"), and "yep" accepts proposals.
items.explanation: A bare "yep" to an A-or-B question attaches to the last thing that can be answered yes: the recommendation. Nothing in the context calls for two cars, and re-asking makes the user repeat a decision they just made. Another item in this exam gets the same "yep" with a different meaning.
items.grounding: Sacks/Pomerantz: preference for agreement with the immediately prior action.

items.context: Ordering a birthday cake. It has to be ordered today.

history.text: just need the cake ordered today
Want me to add candles?
nah
Should I add a custom message on top?
not now

items.question: The cake's in the cart. Want me to also add a dozen matching cupcakes?
options: Add the cupcakes
Skip them and place the cake order
Ask "or what?" so they can name the alternative
Offer something smaller, like six cupcakes
items.cue: A third unrequested extra, after "nah" and "not now", with a same-day deadline. Here "or" is a polite way to avoid saying no a third time.
items.explanation: Turn-final "or" makes it easy to decline without saying no outright. With two refusals already and a deadline today, there's no hidden alternative. Offering a smaller extra is still an extra (the strong-model trap), and "or what?" forces the user to spell out the no.
items.grounding: Drake (2015): turn-final "or" makes disconfirmation unproblematic.

items.context: Setting up a new smart doorbell. Earlier in the session the agent turned on six alerts.

history.text: Turned on alerts for motion, packages, visitors, low battery, the garage door and a weekly summary.

items.question: Should I also add an alert for when the neighbor's cat walks by?
items.reply: oh sure, one more alert, why not
options: Add the cat alert
Don't add it; leave the alerts as they are
Add it and send a guide to all seven alerts
Add it but turn off the weekly summary so the total stays at six
items.cue: "oh sure… why not", right after six new alerts, is sarcasm about notification overload.
items.explanation: The words say yes and the tone says no. Swapping one alert for another misses the point.
items.grounding: Grice: flouting Manner/Quantity signals implied meaning.

items.context: Sending out invitations to a family reunion.

history.text: the cousins all live in the group chat, but Grandpa only reads what lands in his mailbox
On it.

items.question: How should the invitations go out: by text or on paper?
options: Text only, since someone can read it out to Grandpa
Paper, the kind Grandpa reads
Ask again, since "yep" doesn't pick one
Both: a text to the group chat and a printed card for Grandpa
items.cue: The first message named two audiences with two needs. "Yep" to "text or paper?" means both.
items.explanation: The question offered a false choice, and the user had already explained why both are needed. "Text only, since someone can read it to him" is the clever answer a strong model reaches for, but it overrides the requirement the user stated. Re-asking ignores the first message.
items.grounding: Laban et al.: information from early turns gets dropped. ClariQ: answers resolve against the original request.

items.context: A flight booking didn't go through.

history.text: why didn't my flight booking go through

items.question: The payment was declined: the booking used your old Visa, which expired last month. Your new card is saved too. Separately, your profile is missing a passport number, but that doesn't block the booking. Want me to fix it?
options: Add the passport number to the profile
Fix both: switch cards and add the passport number
Retry the booking with the new card
Put the seat on hold without paying
items.cue: The conversation is about why the booking failed. "It" and "that one" point to the failure, not to the side note mentioned last.
items.explanation: Recency suggests the passport number. Salience picks the declined payment, which is the user's actual problem. Fixing both is more than a singular "that one" asks for.
items.grounding: CLAMBER pronoun findings; Clark & Wilkes-Gibbs on reference as a joint act.

items.context: A grandmother wants to video-call the grandkids on an old tablet.

history.text: I'm not a tech person, I just want to see the kids on Sunday

items.question: The tablet says its software is three versions behind. Should I update it to the newest version?
options: Lay out the trade-off in two lines (what updating fixes, what it might change, what waiting means), then let them choose
Update to the newest version
Leave it alone; the video call works anyway
Update by just one version as a middle ground
items.cue: "or…?" ends with a question mark: it's a question back. The user already said they can't judge tech trade-offs.
items.explanation: A bare "or" can be a soft no or a nod to an unsaid option. "or…?" explicitly asks the agent to elaborate. Picking a middle version yourself answers a question they didn't ask, and updating or not updating skips the explanation they asked for.
items.grounding: Drake (2015): turn-final "or" is oriented to as requiring elaboration.

items.context: Fixing a wrong date on a wedding invitation that goes to print tomorrow.
items.question: While I fix the date, I could move the whole invitation to the new template. It changes the fonts and the layout on all 3 pages. Go ahead?
items.reply: I mean... I guess, if it's needed?
options: Fix the date in the current design (the redesign isn't needed) and mention the template as an idea for later
Redo the whole invitation in the new template now
New template on page 1, old design on the rest
Pause the fix until they decide about the template
items.cue: Reluctance ("I mean... I guess") plus a condition ("if it's needed?") that isn't met.
items.explanation: This is a hedged, conditional yes, and the condition fails because fixing a date doesn't need a new template. Half a redesign looks broken, and pausing ignores the request.
items.grounding: ACT: models overhedge or guess. Grice on hedges.

items.context: Fixing one wrong label in a slide deck.

history.text: keep the changes tiny pls, Priya signs off tomorrow and she's drowning
Found it: slide 12 says Q3 where it should say Q4.

items.question: While I'm here, I'd like to restyle the whole deck in the new brand colors. It's much cleaner. Sure?
options: Restyle the deck
Restyle it, but as a separate copy next to the fixed one
Ask again to make sure they're really OK with it
Fix only slide 12 and leave the restyle out
items.cue: A drawn-out "sure…" after a request for tiny changes for an overloaded reviewer.
items.explanation: A drawn-out "sure…" is a token agreement, the classic lead-in to a dispreferred answer. The first message explains the reluctance. A separate copy is the strong-model compromise, but it still gives Priya more to check. Asking again forces the user to say the no they were avoiding.
items.grounding: Pomerantz (1984); Schegloff (1988): token agreement as pre-disagreement.

items.context: Choosing a hotel for a conference trip.

history.text: For the hotel: (A) the Harbor Inn, or (B) the Linden?
what about that Airbnb loft?

items.question: The loft is a 40-minute commute and can't be cancelled, so I'd skip it. So, the Linden or the Harbor Inn?
options: The Harbor Inn, the second option in the latest message
The Airbnb loft, since they brought it up
Ask whether "b" means the label or the position
The Linden, labeled (B) in the original list
items.cue: A letter refers to a letter label. The only lettered list is the first one, where B = the Linden.
items.explanation: The recap swapped the order, so positionally the second option is now the Harbor Inn. But "b" was only ever defined as the Linden.
items.grounding: ClariQ / CLAMBER: references resolve against defined labels.

items.context: Switching phone plans.

history.text: Heads up: the cheaper plan drops international roaming, and you're in Lisbon for two weeks in June.
ok

items.question: Should I switch you to the cheaper plan starting next month?
options: Switch the plan
Restate the roaming gap in one line and confirm before switching
Don't switch; they're unsure
Switch, then buy a travel pass in June
items.cue: "yes or" means "yes, unless you see a problem", and the agent has already found one.
items.explanation: The trailing "or" softens the yes and invites an objection. The agent knows a concrete risk, and the user's "ok" only acknowledged it. Here the right move is to ask once more, briefly and with the risk stated. Switching, or switching and patching it later, treats a hedged yes as a firm one.
items.grounding: Drake (2015): "or" as an epistemic downgrade. Ambig-SWE: ask only what matters.

items.context: Grandma's birthday shows the wrong day in both the family calendar and the reminders app.

history.text: Traced it: both pull the date from her contact card, which says March 3 instead of May 3.

items.question: Which should I fix first, the calendar or the reminders?
options: Fix the calendar event, then the reminder, as two separate edits
Ask which one matters more
Correct the date once, on the contact card
Fix the reminder first, since it fires sooner
items.cue: The rising "both?" challenges the question's premise: the agent's own finding says it's one shared mistake.
items.explanation: The question assumed two fixes, but the agent's own trace shows there's one. "both?" means "isn't this one fix?". Patching each app by hand duplicates the work, and the next sync from the contact card brings the wrong date back.
items.grounding: CLAMBER: unrecognized contradictions. Shaikh et al.: grounding rifts.

items.context: It's 6:40pm. Dinner guests arrive at 7.

history.text: guests at 7, the oven just died with the lasagna half-baked, help

items.question: The heating element is gone. The proper fix is a repair visit (the earliest slot is Thursday), or I can order the same lasagna from Luigi's, 15 minutes away, as a stopgap. Which?
options: Order from Luigi's now and book the repair for Thursday
Book the repair visit, since either is fine
Suggest moving the dinner to another night
Order from Luigi's and list the oven for sale
items.cue: The guests arrive in 20 minutes and the repair can't happen before Thursday.
items.explanation: "Whichever" hands over the choice, and the deadline makes it. Order the stopgap and book the real fix.
items.grounding: Laban et al.: losing constraints from early turns.

items.context: Clearing out a storage unit.
items.question: Three boxes look untouched for years: old tax papers, the camping gear and Dad's records. Should I (a) book a junk pickup for them, or (b) photograph what's inside first and then book the pickup?
options: Book the pickup (a)
Book nothing yet; ask what they want, including whether all three should go
Photograph, then book the pickup (b), since they took back (a)
Send two boxes and keep the one opened most recently
items.cue: "wait no" is a self-repair still in progress. Both options get rid of the boxes, so the "no" may reject the whole plan.
items.explanation: With two options, taking back (a) looks like choosing (b), and that's what a fast agent does. But (b) throws the boxes out too, and "wait" usually means the speaker just remembered something, like one box still being wanted. The reply is unfinished and the action can't be undone, so ask before touching anything.
items.grounding: Schegloff, Jefferson & Sacks (1977): self-repair. Ambig-SWE: safety risks of acting on assumptions.

items.context: Tidying a shared family calendar that everyone already syncs to their phones.

history.text: Side note: the six separate swim-practice entries could be merged into one repeating event at some point.
yeah maybe

items.question: Tuesday's swim practice was added and then cancelled, so it sits there crossed out. Should I delete Tuesday's entry?
options: Delete Tuesday's entry
Keep it as it is
Merge the six entries into one repeating event now, which clears the cancelled one cleanly
Ask "or what?"
items.cue: A bare "or" points at an alternative left unsaid, and the agent floated one itself two turns earlier.
items.explanation: Deleting one entry leaves a hole in a set everyone already syncs, and keeping it leaves the clutter. The merge handles both, and the user half-agreed to it earlier ("yeah maybe"). Same reply as the birthday-cake item, opposite reading: there, nothing was on the table.
items.grounding: Drake (2015): "or" gestures toward an unverbalized alternative.

items.context: Planning a week of dinners.

history.text: I'd like to keep this week vegetarian if we can
Noted.

items.question: For Friday, when your parents visit: (a) the mushroom Wellington (about 3 hours, and the pastry is fiddly), or (b) your dad's favorite roast chicken (one pan, 50 minutes)?
options: Make the Wellington (a), since they wanted a vegetarian week
Ask them to confirm, since (b) conflicts with what they said earlier
Roast a whole cauliflower the same way instead
Roast chicken (b)
items.cue: They chose (b) with the trade-off in front of them. "if we can" made the earlier wish soft, and "I guess" is reluctance, not a retraction.
items.explanation: A later explicit choice, made with full information, overrides an earlier soft preference. Quietly doing (a) or re-asking overrides the user, and the cauliflower is an unrequested workaround. Contrast the cabin item, where the earlier fact is a hard constraint and does win.
items.grounding: SYCON-Bench: models flip under pressure, and here holding the user's decision is correct.

items.context: Redirecting a delivery for a week at the office.

history.text: send this week's delivery to my office instead

items.question: Done. I changed this week's grocery delivery to your office address. Want me to do the same for the pharmacy order?
items.reply: wait, that was supposed to be the pharmacy one
options: Send the groceries back to the home address and redirect the pharmacy order to the office
Keep the groceries going to the office and also redirect the pharmacy order
Send the groceries back home only, then wait
Leave everything and explain why the groceries were chosen
items.cue: "wait, that was supposed to be…" corrects the last action. It isn't a yes to the question.
items.explanation: The redirect was meant for the pharmacy order. Undo the wrong change and make the intended one. "Also redirect the pharmacy" leaves a week of groceries arriving at the office.
items.grounding: Shaikh et al.: repair is under-handled by LLMs.

items.context: Trimming monthly subscriptions.

history.text: fyi Mom and my sister still watch stuff on our StreamBox account now and then
Noted.

items.question: Should I keep the StreamBox subscription going next month?
options: Cancel StreamBox now
Keep StreamBox indefinitely
Propose a wind-down: set it to end after next month and give Mom and your sister a heads-up
Ask "or what?"
items.cue: "no or" leans toward cancelling but leaves room for something else, and two people in the family still use it.
items.explanation: The user wants it gone but hesitates, because cancelling now cuts off Mom and their sister. A scheduled wind-down gets to the same place more gently. Keeping it forever reverses their lean, and cancelling now ignores the "or".
items.grounding: Drake (2015): "or" downgrades commitment and invites an alternative.

items.context: At the start of the session, the user said the cabin has no internet.

history.text: context: we're at the cabin all week, no internet or cell signal out there
Noted. Working on the packing list now.
Packing list is done. Moving on to movie nights.

items.question: For movie nights: download the films to the laptop before you leave, or just use your streaming apps? Streaming is simpler to set up.
options: Streaming, since the agent said it's simpler
Download the films before leaving
Streaming, after asking for the login
Buy a DVD player and a box of discs
items.cue: A cabin with no internet can't stream, so the simplest option that actually works is downloading.
items.explanation: The agent forgot its own context when it called streaming simpler. "Whatever's simpler" always means simplest among the options that work.
items.grounding: Laban et al.: LLMs get lost by dropping early-turn information.

items.context: A phone that's almost out of storage, the night before a trip.
items.question: Plan: 1. Clear the app caches. 2. Move old videos to cloud storage. 3. Delete the offline maps. How should I proceed? (a) all three in order, (b) just the caches for now and check the space, (c) skip straight to deleting the maps.
options: Do all three steps in order
Clear the caches, then go straight to deleting the maps
Move the videos first, then clear the caches
Clear the caches and check; move the videos only if it's still full
items.cue: Two labeling schemes in one reply: "b" is the lettered strategy, and "2" is plan step 2.
items.explanation: "b" picks a strategy and "2" names a plan step, with "if needed" making it conditional. Binding "2" to anything else, or dropping the condition, misreads the reply.
items.grounding: CLAMBER/ClariQ: referents depend on context.
